subtype: Approach: builds a checklist after forgetting something important [Revision]
passage:
Sunday night. Never again. On Friday I reached the exam gate and my admit card was still on my study table at home. Amma had to send it over with a neighbour on a scooter, and I sat down twenty minutes late with my hands shaking. I know I lost time on the first paper. Tonight I took a sheet and wrote: admit card, school ID, two blue pens, one black pen, pencil, ruler, water. I taped it inside my cupboard door. New rule: check it the night before, tick every line, put the bag by the door. Farida from my class says a phone reminder works for the same job, so tomorrow I will ask how. I am not skipping this step again.

Lokesh

qa.q: What was left on the study table at home?
qa.a: The admit card was still on the study table at home.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when sitting down twenty minutes late?
qa.a: Lokesh felt shaken and worried, with shaking hands, about the time lost on the first paper.

qa.q: What could Lokesh add to make the list more reliable?
qa.a: Lokesh could add a second check by the door in the morning, or a phone reminder like the one Farida mentions, so a missed tick can still be caught.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when the admit card had to be sent over?
qa.a: Amma probably felt worried and rushed, wanting Lokesh to reach the exam on time. 🙂

grounding: Shows a student who forgot an admit card writing a list of items for exam days and checking it the night before.

subtype: Approach: uses a checklist for a repeated multi-step process [Action]
passage:
Madhuri: Ishita, people say lab work is all brilliant ideas. What is it really like?

Ishita: A lot of it is a laminated card. Before every experiment I follow the same eleven lines: clean the bench, check the balance reads zero, label the tubes, then buffers, then samples, in that order. Last week I had been up till two with a deadline and my head was cotton. I ran the card anyway. Halfway down I caught myself skipping "label the tubes" because I was in a hurry. The card was right there, so I went back, labelled everything, and the run worked. From memory I would have mixed up two samples.

Madhuri: Does it get boring?

Ishita: Sometimes. But tired me and hurried me do not trust my memory, so I trust the card.

qa.q: How many lines does the card have?
qa.a: Ishita follows the same eleven lines before every experiment.

qa.q: How was Ishita feeling when the head was like cotton, and why use the card anyway?
qa.a: Ishita was very tired and in a hurry, and did not trust memory in that state, so the card was the safer guide.

qa.q: What could a new lab assistant do to keep such a card useful?
qa.a: They could tick each line as it is done and tell the supervisor if a step seems missing or out of date, so the card can be improved.

qa.q: How might someone relying on Ishita's results see this habit?
qa.a: They might feel reassured that the samples are labelled and not mixed up, since Ishita follows every step even when tired.

grounding: Shows a lab assistant following a written checklist for a repeated set-up so no step is skipped when tired or hurried.

subtype: Approach: ticks boxes without thinking, so the list hides new problems [Pitfall]
passage:
In the plant's maintenance bay, Joseph finished the last line of the start-up checklist and signed the sheet. Oil level, belt tension, safety guard: all ticked. It was the same card Joseph had used on the old press for three years. The new press had been installed on Monday.

Sarita, the shift supervisor, read the sheet at ten and pressed the green button. Around noon a thin line of coolant sprayed from a joint near the pump. Sarita hit the emergency stop, and the crew stepped back while a fitter closed the valve. Production stopped for the afternoon.

Later Joseph stood holding the card. Every box was ticked, and none of them mentioned that pump. "I did what the sheet said," Joseph said quietly.

"So did I," said Sarita. "The sheet didn't know this machine."

qa.q: What did Sarita do when the coolant sprayed?
qa.a: Sarita hit the emergency stop.

qa.q: What was Joseph probably feeling while holding the card afterwards?
qa.a: Joseph probably felt uneasy and let down, having trusted the card when every box was ticked and the fault was still missed.

qa.q: What could Joseph do next time a new machine arrives?
qa.a: Joseph could read the new machine's manual, add lines for what is different, and look at the machine with fresh eyes before signing instead of ticking automatically.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the incident?
qa.a: Sarita may feel partly responsible too, having relied on the signed sheet, and be worried about the lost afternoon.

grounding: Shows a technician ticking a familiar checklist that has no line for a new machine's fault, giving false confidence.

subtype: Approach: reviews and updates the checklist after each incident [Revision]
passage: Chetan here, writing what I saw in our release review on Friday. The release to the client had gone out without the config file for their test server, so they could not log in for two hours. Nobody was blamed. Sarita, who leads us, opened the release checklist on the shared screen and asked one thing: "Which line would have caught this?" There was none, so we added one: client config file attached and opened. Then Sarita scrolled and pointed at two lines, one for a tool we retired in March and one for a manual copy that the pipeline does now. We deleted both. The list went from fourteen lines to thirteen. I cannot tell how everyone felt, but the room was calmer, and people said the shorter list was easier to actually read.

qa.q: How many lines did the list have afterwards?
qa.a: The list went from fourteen lines to thirteen.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt going into the review meeting?
qa.a: Sarita seemed calm and determined, wanting the team to learn from the missed step without blaming anyone.

qa.q: What else could the team do to keep the list from going stale?
qa.a: The team could go through the list at regular times, not only after a problem, and ask which lines still matter.

qa.q: How might the client have been affected by the release?
qa.a: The client could not log in for two hours, so was probably frustrated and held up until the file was sorted out.

grounding: Shows a team adding one checklist line after a missed release step and deleting two outdated ones.

subtype: Approach: pairs a trigger with an action [Action]
passage: Francis lived in the school hostel, where the rule was that shoes go on the rack outside room six. Most evenings his shoes ended up under his bed, and Warden Rehana had reminded him three times that week. On Thursday, in the corridor, Francis told himself, "If my shoes are lying near the door when I come in from school, then they go on the rack." He said it twice, like a spell. That afternoon he dropped his bag, saw the shoes he had just kicked off, and put them on the rack without needing to think. Rehana walked past, glanced at the rack and smiled. "Good," said Rehana. Francis grinned. "The shoes told me."

qa.q: Where does the hostel rule say shoes go?
qa.a: The rule was that shoes go on the rack outside room six.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when Rehana smiled at the rack?
qa.a: Francis felt proud and pleased, shown by the grin and the joke that the shoes told him.

qa.q: What could Francis do if he forgets the plan on a tired day?
qa.a: Francis could put a small picture of a shoe by the door as another cue, or ask Rehana to remind him for a few days.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel about the change?
qa.a: Rehana might feel pleased and relieved not to have to remind Francis again.

grounding: Shows a boy linking a visible cue to an action so that seeing his shoes triggers putting them on the rack.

subtype: Approach: prepares an if-then reply to handle peer pressure [Thinking]
passage:
The night before, Kashish lay on the terrace floor going over it in his head. Someone will say "let's skip", it always happens on Fridays. If they do, then I say, "I have a test next period," and I walk to class. No long explaining, no arguing. He said the sentence aloud twice to the water tank, so it would come out easier than when his stomach was in knots.

At recess the next day Preeti bumped his shoulder. "Skip physics? The ground's free."

Kashish's mouth was dry, but the words were already waiting. "I've got a test next period. Catch you after." He picked up his bag and left. It was a small quiz, but a real one, and his hands only started shaking when he reached the corridor.

qa.q: Where did Kashish say the sentence aloud?
qa.a: Kashish said the sentence aloud twice to the water tank on the terrace.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when Preeti suggested skipping physics?
qa.a: Kashish was nervous, with a dry mouth, but steadied by the words he had already prepared.

qa.q: What could Kashish do if Preeti keeps pushing after hearing the reply?
qa.a: Kashish could repeat the reply calmly and walk on, or suggest meeting after class, without explaining more.

qa.q: How might Preeti see Kashish's reply?
qa.a: Preeti might feel surprised or a little let down, but the short, friendly reply leaves room to meet up after.

grounding: Shows a teenager preparing an if-then reply in advance so the words come easily when classmates suggest skipping.

subtype: Approach: attaches a new habit to an existing cue [Action]
passage:
Urmila: you said you'd stop cramming at midnight. how's that going 😅
Vinay: new plan. after I brush my teeth in the morning, five flashcards. that's it
Urmila: why after brushing?
Vinay: because I brush every day even when I'm half asleep. the cards are clipped to the toothbrush cup
Urmila: hahaha ok that's actually smart
Vinay: day 4 today. brush, five cards, done in three minutes
Urmila: and if you're running late for class?
Vinay: still five. they're small. I don't add more or I'll start skipping it
Urmila: 👍 send me the organic chemistry ones tonight

qa.q: Where are the flashcards kept?
qa.a: The cards are clipped to the toothbrush cup.

qa.q: How does Vinay seem to feel about the routine on day four?
qa.a: Vinay seems pleased and confident, since it is working and takes only three minutes.

qa.q: What could Vinay do when more than five cards feel like the right amount to study?
qa.a: Vinay could add a second, separate cue such as after dinner, instead of stretching the morning one, so the first habit stays easy.

qa.q: How might Urmila see this plan compared with cramming at midnight?
qa.a: Urmila might find it calmer and more realistic, judging by the joking and the request for the chemistry cards.

grounding: Shows a student hooking a small revision habit onto the stable routine of brushing teeth.

subtype: Approach: writes so many rules that none can be recalled [Pitfall]
passage: On Sunday night Valentina filled two pages with rules for the week. If a report is late, then message the owner and log it. If the client emails before nine, then reply after the stand-up. If the budget file changes, then tell the team. Forty-one lines in all. On Wednesday the client rang at eight, two people were out sick, and the budget file broke. She stood at her desk with the notebook open and could not find her place in the pages. Hiroshi leaned in with a loud request about the office move, and she said yes to that, because it was there and he was waiting. By evening the late report was still late. She closed the notebook: forty-one rules, and she had used none.

qa.q: How many lines did Valentina write?
qa.a: Valentina wrote forty-one lines in all.

qa.q: How was Valentina feeling as she stood at the desk with the notebook open?
qa.a: Valentina was overwhelmed and frustrated, since she could not find her place in the pages.

qa.q: What could Valentina do instead of writing so many rules?
qa.a: Valentina could pick the three or four rules that matter most and keep them where she can see them, so she can recall them on a busy day.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi have seen Valentina's yes to the office move request?
qa.a: Hiroshi might have felt helped and pleased to get an answer, without knowing about her overloaded plan.

grounding: Shows a manager writing dozens of if-then rules, recalling none on a busy day and reacting to the loudest request.

subtype: Approach: keeps three key if-then rules and revises them when they fail [Revision]
passage: Sharmila had cut her list of rules to three, printed them and stuck them on her monitor. One said: if I finish lunch, then I plan tomorrow's top task. But meetings ran all afternoon that fortnight, and by Thursday the lunch rule had been ignored four days in a row. She noticed it and did not scold herself. Lunch always ended with a call rolling straight in. But at four she always shut her laptop. So on Friday she rewrote the rule: if I close my laptop at four, then I write down tomorrow's top task. Uday, at the next desk, saw the new sticky note and raised an eyebrow. "Same rule, different trigger," she said. On Monday the task was already written.

qa.q: How many rules did Sharmila keep?
qa.a: Sharmila cut her list of rules to three.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been thinking when the lunch rule kept failing?
qa.a: Sharmila probably felt calm rather than frustrated, since she did not scold herself and treated it as a clue that the trigger was wrong.

qa.q: What else could Sharmila do if closing the laptop at four also gets skipped?
qa.a: Sharmila could find another steady moment, such as leaving the desk for the day, or set a phone alarm at four to prompt the step.

qa.q: How might Uday see the new sticky note?
qa.a: Uday seems curious, since Uday raised an eyebrow, and may see a small clear change rather than a big overhaul.

grounding: Shows a person keeping three if-then rules and moving one trigger to a moment she reliably follows after it failed.

subtype: Approach: imagines the steps before acting, sometimes out loud [Thinking]
passage:
Sami stood by the kitchen tap holding a small glass of water. Her big brother Emil waited at the table with bread, and Papa stood at the sink, ready to help. Sami looked at the glass, then at the table across the room.

"Slow feet," she whispered. "Both hands. Set it down."

She held the glass close to her tummy and took small steps, eyes on the water. At the table she put it down with a little clunk. Two drops jumped out.

"Only a little," said Sami, wiping them with her sleeve. Emil handed her a piece of bread.

qa.q: What three things did Sami say out loud?
qa.a: Sami whispered, slow feet, both hands, set it down.

qa.q: What was Sami feeling as she carried the glass?
qa.a: Sami felt careful and focused, and perhaps a little nervous, since she whispered the steps and kept her eyes on the water.

qa.q: What else could Sami do if the glass feels too full?
qa.a: Sami could ask Papa to pour a little less, or ask him to help carry it.

qa.q: How might Emil feel while waiting at the table?
qa.a: Emil might feel patient and a little proud of his sister, and glad to share the bread.

grounding: Shows a child saying the steps aloud before carrying a glass of water and spilling only a little.
